title: The Supreme Court First Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Shrunk Them: From Flag Salutes to Backpack Searches
dek: From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six rulings trace the arc of public school students' constitutional rights; the Court, having declared that 'schools are not totalitarian enclaves,' also upheld corporal punishment and searches based on reasonable suspicion, narrowing the boundaries of those rights.
why: Each ruling is explained in five or six minutes, covering background and key holdings—ideal for listeners who want a single overview of the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment, and backpack searches in American public schools.
who: Parents, middle and high school teachers, law students, and anyone curious about the limits of government power and children's rights in American public schools.
skip: If you're familiar with the Establishment Clause, you can skip the second case; if you know the earlier cases well, jump to the corporal punishment and search cases after 25:40.

points.h: The Flag Salute Case: Students' Rights Enter the Schoolhouse
points.body: Can students really claim First Amendment rights during the school day? This case actually began with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families believed saluting the flag violated the commandments against other gods and graven images, so they refused to salute or pledge. In 1940, the Supreme Court ruled against them, and World War II led more districts to require daily salutes and pledges. West Virginia expelled students who refused to recite the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and fined or jailed their parents. In 1943, the Court reversed 6–3, with Justice Jackson writing on Flag Day: no official can define orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion, or other opinions; students need not confess words that contradict their hearts or make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students have some First Amendment rights inside school.

During the Cold War, America cast itself as a God-fearing nation, adding 'Under God' to the Pledge in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951, New York's Board of Regents asked religious leaders to compose a short, interfaith prayer, leaving adoption to local districts. The district that implemented it allowed students to opt out, but parents of ten students sued anyway. In 1962, Engel v. Vitale struck it down 6–1; the key was not coercion but that the prayer was government-written, itself constituting an establishment of religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: 'It is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties'; the same power that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of all other religions could easily establish one sect of Christianity. The decision sparked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families faced ridicule and harassment.

In December 1965, Des Moines middle and high school students planned to wear black armbands to class to protest US involvement in Vietnam. The school announced in advance that those who refused to remove them would be suspended; some students—including four siblings—wore them and were suspended. In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7–2. The issue was not ordinary dress code but a quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Absent evidence of actual or reasonably foreseeable material disruption, schools could not suppress student opinion. The opinion declared that public schools are not totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This 'substantial disruption' test became the benchmark for campus speech. Justice Black dissented, predicting students would resist nearly all rules; the hosts note that this slippery-slope argument sounds quite absurd.

In 1983, Hazelwood East High School's student newspaper, The Spectrum, had two articles that troubled Principal Reynolds: one on teen pregnancy used pseudonyms but might still identify the interviewee, and a divorce story named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to delete the entire two pages rather than just the articles, citing lack of time to edit and the need to publish before semester's end. In 1988, the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5–3. The key distinction was between 'tolerating student speech' and 'promoting student speech': the paper was funded by the school, readers would assume school endorsement, and the articles were indeed immature in journalistic ethics. The Court held that schools may regulate content they promote. This drew the first clear boundary around Tinker's rights.

points.h: Corporal Punishment Is Not Cruel and Unusual
points.body: Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks when she was young, and research shows corporal punishment has not disappeared in America. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's regulation paddle was less than two feet long, three to four inches wide, and half an inch thick, with one to five strokes per incident; but Ingram was hit more than 20 times in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Court did not decide whether the individual punishment was excessive; it ruled that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The Eighth Amendment protects convicted persons; prisoners and schoolchildren are separated by 'the harsh fact of criminal conviction and incarceration.' Schools are open places with teachers and peers as witnesses, and students go home at the end of the day. According to NEA statistics, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practiced in 14; boys, Black students, and students with disabilities are struck at significantly higher rates.

points.h: Backpack Searches Need Only Reasonable Suspicion
points.body: In 1980, a 14-year-old New Jersey student, TLO, was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice Principal Choplik searched her purse, found cigarettes and rolling papers, then continued searching and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing. TLO was convicted and sentenced to one year of probation. In 1985, the Supreme Court upheld the search 6–3. The Court acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment applies to school officials and that students have a legitimate expectation of privacy, but it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. Therefore, school searches need not meet the probable cause standard required for police; they only need the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion. The teacher's report gave the vice principal reason to suspect TLO had cigarettes, and the purse was the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was also reasonable.

terms.def: The threshold established in Tinker for disciplining student speech: there must be actual material disruption or evidence that disruption would reasonably occur.

A lower evidentiary standard than probable cause, applied to school officials' searches of students and their belongings.

Students in school as well as out of school are persons under our Constitution.
